newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street banks on Republicans holding Congress.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street banks on Republicans holding Congress.

text.p: For months, Wall Street has viewed the re-election of President Bill Clinton this November as almost inevitable, so much so that when Republican Presidential candidate Bob Dole said he favored a 15 percent tax cut, the financial markets dismissed the prospect as moot.
But what Wall Street has not been banking on is a shift in the control of Congress, an outcome pollsters and analysts now say is not out of the question.

"The markets have been too complacent in assuming the Senate and the House will remain under GOP control and keep an expected Clinton Administration in check," said Josh Stiles, senior bond strategist at I.D.E.A., a consulting firm.
Political experts say chances are evenly split for a Democratic comeback in the House, a result that would require Democrats to win a net gain of eighteen new seats.
A Democratic majority in the Senate is seen as less likely, but not impossible.
Wall Street analysts said financial markets would react negatively to a Democratic sweep on Election Day.
"If both Houses of Congress shifted to Democratic control, that would be a bit negative for the bond market," said Josh Feinman, vice president and global markets economist at Bankers Trust.
Feinman said the market would be concerned that the Democrats, unfettered by Republican majorities in Congress, could embark on a more aggressive ideological agenda.
The prospect of a Republican White House with a Republican Congress might also arouse concern, Feinman said.
Though Democratic party ideology has gradually evolved toward fiscal conservatism, "traders would (still) fret over (the potential for) a gradual reversion to 'tax and spend' ways," said Stiles.

"Democratic gains in Congress would be negative, certainly, but not deeply negative -- unless both houses went over to the Democrats," said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc.
Moran said if Democrats won both houses of Congress, "you would see a pronounced jump in interest rates -- a quarter to a half of a percentage point."
If just the House of Representatives went Democratic, the 30-year long bond yield would rise a more modest 10 to 20 basis points, reflecting "risk on the deficit front," he said.
Moran said the chairmen that would head committees in a Democratic House and guide new legislation through Congress "would be among the most liberal in decades."

Steve Ricchuito, chief financial economist at BZW Securities, said the market would be "very disappointed" if the Democrats won the House. He said the market assumes the Republicans will retain the House of Representatives, even if it is just by a slim majority.
Some people also expect the Republicans to strengthen their position in the Senate, he said.

"A lot depends on what leadership takes over in the House and how they delegate (committee) chairmanships," Ricchuito said. "If they go strictly by seniority, the market will be very upset because the Democrats with a lot of seniority tend to be liberal."
William Sullivan, senior vice president and economist at Dean Witter Reynolds, said the market has priced in a Clinton victory -- "no ifs, ands or buts."
But Sullivan said the market's current pricing structure "doesn't allow for a turnover of control of either the House or the Senate."
The loss of GOP majorities in Congress "would seem to point to a more liberal bias on Capitol Hill -- to the detriment of bonds," he said.
While analysts agreed that Wall Street is unprepared for Democratic majorities on Capitol Hill, some said the negative reaction to the change might not last long.

"The market would have a very short-lived, negative reaction," said Elliott Platt, managing director, economic research, at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp. "I think the market remembers that it was the Clinton program that did lower budget deficits."
Sullivan of Dean Witter said a Democratic victory on Capitol Hill would not be a sea change for the market.

"We won't even know the agenda of the new Congress until it convenes in January, so there can be two months of debate on (the significance of) the power shift that will be nothing more than hot air," he said.
"The basic trend for the rest of the year will be shaped by the economic and inflation data," he added. "Bonds will do better even in the face of some Congressional power realignment."
And Platt contended that an all-Democratic government might be better for bonds than an all-Republican environment.

"The Clinton Administration is very committed to fiscal responsibility," said Platt. "I would worry more about a Bob Dole presidency in which we had a massive tax cut with no clear indications as to how it was going to be paid for. That would be a concern if Dole were elected."
